newsitem.title: USA: Senate votes to ban U.S. funds for suicide help.
newsitem.headline: Senate votes to ban U.S. funds for suicide help.

text.p: The Senate voted unanimously on Wednesday to ban federal funds for doctor-assisted suicide, injecting Congress into an emotional debate over whether there should be a right to die.

The measure, passed 99-0, was largely symbolic because no state allows assisted suicide and no federal program pays for it. The House passed the same bill April 10, 398-16, so it now goes to President Bill Clinton, who was expected to sign it.
But the U.S. Supreme Court was considering two cases that could establish a constitutional right to assisted suicide or pave the way for states to legalize it. A ruling was expected by July.

"We want to send a signal to Dr. Kevorkian we don't agree with him," said Oklahoma Republican Sen. Don Nickles, referring to the Michigan pathologist who has helped a number of ill people end their lives.
"Tax dollars used for health care purposes ought to be used to extend life, not end life," said North Dakota Democratic Sen. Byron Dorgan.
The legislation bars use of federal health care or other funds to pay for or promote assisted suicide. It does not prevent states from adopting laws to allow aided suicide.
The measure would not prevent terminally ill people from refusing medical treatment, food or fluids as they neared the end of life, options that have become widely acceptable in U.S. society.

It also would not bar patients from getting pain medication, even though some drugs can slow breathing and may hasten death. Doctors and ethicists recognize a distinction between drugs meant to control pain and large doses of drugs meant to end life.
"Assisted suicide is a form of killing. If we allow federal funding of this horrific act, then we risk minimizing the importance of life," said Missouri Republican Sen. Kit Bond.

Advocates of assisted suicide say mentally competent, terminally ill patients should have the right to decide when they are ready to die and to get the help they need to carry out that decision in a humane, dignified manner.

Critics, including the American Medical Association and other leading health groups, say doctors should help ease their patients' emotional and physical pain, not help kill them. Some also say there is a danger that legal suicide could lead to abuse and that patients could be coerced.

Anti-abortion groups have also joined the drive against assisted suicide, and the National Right to Life Committee called the bill "a crucial pre-emptive strike to prevent tax dollars of American citizens from being used to fund legalized killing."
